findings.title: Blocked email check is case-sensitive and easily bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` lookup, and the value passed here is the raw `user.email` attribute, which is stored as the user typed it (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] directly, no downcasing). A blocked address like spammer@example.com can register as Spammer@Example.com and sail past the block list, since PostgreSQL string comparison is case-sensitive. The email should be normalized (e.g. Email.downcase) before the lookup, both here and wherever BlockedEmail records are created.

findings.title: Blocked emails not enforced on change_email
findings.body: The new BlockedEmail validation only runs via User's `email` validator, but `change_email` never saves the user with the new email — it only checks uniqueness and creates an email token; the token confirmation path (EmailToken.confirm) updates the address without going through the new validator. An existing account (or one created before an address was blocked) can switch to a blocked email address, defeating the feature. The block check should also be applied in the email-change flow.

findings.title: Match statistics update is racy and performed inside a validation
findings.body: should_block? reads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, and saves, which loses increments under concurrent signups; more notably it is called from EmailValidator#validate_each, so merely validating a User (not saving) performs a database write with `record.save`, whose failure is silently ignored. Use an atomic update (e.g. update_counters / UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) and consider moving the stats update out of the validation path.

findings.title: rejectedEmails comparison is exact-string and won't match case variants
findings.body: After a failed signup the server echoes back result.values.email and it is pushed into rejectedEmails; the check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` is an exact string comparison against the current accountEmail input. If the user retries with different casing (e.g. Bad@Spam.com vs bad@spam.com) the client-side rejection won't trigger and they'll get another full server round-trip each time. Compare lowercased values.
